utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Sarah Clanton, case manager Thomas Laugel, legal interns, Katherine Davis and Lucy Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic, Christopher Gosnell, case manager Negosava Smiljanic, and intern, Philipp Muller. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, yesterday you spoke about the signing of that document which was supposed to initiate a cease-fire, and you also told us that some government members and some other people were against the signing of that document. Do you remember any of them, any of those who were against?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I told you that I consulted the government members who were in Borovo Selo. However, when I returned to Dalj, a group of people from Dalj was waiting for me there. They attacked me, verbally. The secretary of the local commune of Dalj, Milan Panisic cursed both me and Milosevic. He told me that I was stupid, that I didn't understand anything, that I had to insist on signing as the prime minister because, in that case, we would be given statehood and independence. In my view, it was an utopia, it was nonsense. But I didn't want to the quarrel when I just left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, what was your relationship with this gentleman whom you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never quarreled with anybody. I didn't curse anybody. I didn't allow anybody to curse me. That's why I didn't want to talk to him. From then on, I never even greeted him in passing. But I did not come across him that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat his family name or, rather, his full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Panisic, nicknamed Miso.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please P194.140. It is tab 152.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you spoke in great detail about this document. Did you try in any way to obtain the original of that document once you saw it, once you realised that it existed in the course of this trial?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that I didn't sign this document. This order was impossible. When I saw the signature, it did seem like my signature, but it seems to have been executed in two goes; first the name and then the family name. That's why I insisted with my Defence team to try and get hold of the original. And also I was interested in the origin or the source of that document, who was it who submitted it. But then I heard that it was provided by the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of the search for the original?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there was no original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please 1D75. It is tab 728. It should not be broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you proceed, Mr. Zivanovic, I'm wondering whether the -- this may have been explored when this document was first exhibited, but my question is whether the witness has any comment to make on what appears to be a seal at the left of the signature in the original -- well, the "original" document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether there is a copy where the seal is more visible. However, from what I see here, I could not discern the type of seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because -- because there were some other documents which were also suspicious. The seals on them differed from the one used by the government. I can't remember whether this seal is visible or more visible somewhere else. I -- I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please 1D75. It is tab 728. May we see next page, please. In English it is next page, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember that we received -- do you remember that this document was attached to the reply to our request?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that it says that there is no original in the archives, in the state archives, that this document doesn't exist?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, object to it. We object to it, Mr. President. This witness is not able to provide foundation. We would need to hear someone -- from someone who was actually involved in searching for it. Thank you. That's our objection: No foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that there is no foundation for this document. Many documents were tendered without giving evidence of the author of this document or such document or someone else. It is document that's -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This, Mr. President, is a response from the government of the Republic of Serbia to a Request for Assistance that went across from the Defence. So it's not actually providing documents, which is the normal thing that happens in response to RFAs. Rather, it's saying that a document wasn't found. Any witness could sit in the box and say, as this witness just did, "Yes, that's what the letter says." But it doesn't really provide any sort of foundation for us to determine what, in fact, is the point here, which is whether the letter was found, where it was looked for, what was done in order to locate it. And this witness is not in a position to answer those questions, I don't think, and that's why, in our view, there is an insufficient foundation for this letter to be admitted for the assertion that the letter is, in fact, not to be found in the possession of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, do you want to reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just add that this document -- this document clearly, clearly states that such document is not available in the archives of -- in the state archives of Serbia and that we were not able to provide the original to see whether the signature of Mr. Hadzic is authentic on the original of this document or it is -- it was false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection is overruled. The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 1D75 will become Exhibit D128, under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please 1D186. It is tab 733. It should not be broadcasted, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Next page in English. Or the third page of English translation. [Interpretation] We can go to the following page in the original as well. I believe that the translated version also needs to be moved to the following page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, we object on the same grounds. The witness for this is a representative of the government of Serbia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Noted and overruled.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D129, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you remember that the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem in the summer of 1991 issued a declaration on the general mobilisation of the citizens who were at the time in Serbia, Vojvodina; i.e., in Yugoslavia as a whole?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please P166. It is tab 125. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the screen you can see at the bottom of the original that there was, indeed, a declaration on mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, but just barely. Can it be zoomed in? Because I can only see the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you scroll down on the original? Yes. And a little bit on right side. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember this declaration on general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. It was published in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me why was it that the government declared general mobilisation at the time? Was it at a request by a state organ of either Serbia, Yugoslavia, or was there any other reason for that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was nobody's request. The residents of the district who were there in the territory didn't need any mobilisation. They were already there, and they responded to the call-up. But the problem was with the Serbs who had fled leaving behind their homes and mostly elderly parents, whereas they went to Serbia and lived there with their children. They were over 18, mature people, fit for combat. We, the government, knew from their neighbours in those villages that these people were not willing to take care of their homes and elderly parents, and they asked us that we send an appeal through the media for them to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was the reason why the government made that decision and that proclamation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only reason. Because it was a big problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see 1D3021. It is tab 1121.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would -- Mr. Zivanovic, would this be confidential and not to be broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I see that it was provided under Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report dated 8 August 1991 from a meeting held by a Working Group of the Presidency of the SFRY. Do you know about this meeting? Because I see it included some representatives of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Do you know this meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Koncarevic told me later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 5, it is said that the persons detained will be exchanged based on lists previously received by the commission, and they would be released by 1800 hours and work should be resumed. Do you remember, was this decision implemented?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was. I don't know if it was in this specific case, but I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender 1D3021 into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D134, Your Honours. Should it be under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Under seal, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to say that for some of these FBIS articles they were subsequently declassified or the Rule 70 protection was lifted. And that's why some of these are not being -- coming into evidence under seal, and so we're going to check on this specific one but it may be that it would no longer be covered by Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll hear from you, Mr. Stringer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Hadzic, that on the 16th or 15th of August there was an all-for-all prisoner exchange?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see P2988, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is tab 667.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that you also attended one meeting at Borovo Selo when this Working Group from the Presidency arrived and that alongside you there were Koncarevic, Petrovic, and Kojic. Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it because Drazen Budisa and Zivko Milosevic were also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this all-for-all prisoner exchange, referred to in paragraph 1, took place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. But it is not correctly written at the top. It should be "Jusgo," Zivko Juzbasic and Drazen Budisa. Zivko Juzbasic and Drazen Budisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who was holding those prisoners -- or, rather, who decided which people should be exchanged out of the total of prisoners who were held in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was all decided by federal institutions; that is to say, the Presidency, our government, the federal Executive Council, and the JNA carried out their decisions. When I said "our government," I meant the federal government of Yugoslavia. That means no comma. And then in our record, I see that there is a comma after the words "our government," followed by the federal Executive Council, so it looks like there were several governments involved. I meant our federal government. We were at that time a part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the JNA set up a commission to deal with cease-fires and exchanges of persons detained in interethnic conflicts in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: P2921. It is tab 656. P2921. It is tab [Microphone not activated]. Okay, we'll skip it. It is not this document. Yeah. That's correct. That's correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have seen this document before during the trial. I'd like to know if you had been aware of the work of this commission?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that it had been established, but I didn't have this paper and didn't know any details. Nobody informed us in any form.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see P2915, please. It is tab 1310.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document deals with an exchange that took place in Klisa. And if you look at the second paragraph, you will see that, in addition to members of the EU mission and JNA officers, this meeting was also attended by two ministers from the government of SBWS. Can you tell us, what was the role of these ministers, and tell us their names, if you can remember. But what was their role in these talks and negotiations about the exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On behalf of SBWS, this commission was assisted by Ilija Koncarevic, but I'm confused when I see this reference to two ministers from the government. Koncarevic's job was to make a list of Serbs based on missing person reports from their families so they could be exchanged for Croats. These Serbs were from Vinkovci, Osijek, et cetera. So his job was to make the list, or help make the list. He had no other role. And these two ministers, I suppose, were Slavko Dokmanovic, who was a minister, and Rade Leskovac, who was a deputy minister. I believe they were at these talks in Klisa because they were making lists of Serbs for the municipality of Vukovar. Serbs from our villages who were either captured or were left behind on the Croatian side when the war broke out so they couldn't go home anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look now at document 2955.2913, tab 64. Could we zoom in on the original a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is about a press conference held on the 19th or 20th September, we can't see the date clearly, where you spoke among other people. Could we look at what you said there; that is to say, the first two paragraphs. Sorry, that was after the contribution by Petrovic, paragraph number 5. No, the fourth paragraph. This is a question put to you by the correspondent of TASS news agency. It quotes you as saying, I will quote: "... his government offered to the Croatian authorities 20 captured members of the guard in exchange for the missing Soviet journalists ..." It seems to follow from this that the government of SBWS was holding some 20 members of the Croatian Home Guards they were offering in exchange to the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of SBWS never held a single prisoner. When I said "the government," I meant the government of our state, the federal government. That's what Ilija Koncarevic told me. They were offering 20 Croatian Guards. And the answer from the Croats was that they didn't know about those two captured Russians. If they had known, they would have probably exchanged them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems to follow from this text that you said at this conference "my government." Was this correctly reported?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. First of all, I never used the words "my government" even talking about the government of SBWS. It was not my government. This reference here is to our federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since this conference was also filmed and we have seen the footage here in the courtroom, I should like us to look at this again, and I want you to see if you can recognise the words you've uttered then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is P40, tab 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the document number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is Exhibit P40, tab 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab 27 seems to have another exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I know -- no, sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The issue of western borders of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem is open. This was said by the president of the government of these regions, Goran Hadzic, in his talks with journalists in the Belgrade international press centre. On this occasion, he reminded about the proposal of the Serb National Council of these areas to, if need be, establish this border with the help of moving Croatian and Serb population in the broader area. "Reporter: Serb Autonomous Region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem is no longer in Croatia. The issue of western borders is open and the government of this Serb autonomous region advocates a democratic way of solving this and by respecting the will of the people. "Goran Hadzic, president of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, said this to local and foreign journalists in the international press centre in Belgrade. Information minister, Ilija Petrovic, reminded the borders, according to the London agreement are Ilova, Moslavina, Virovitica, and then also, at the proposal of the National Council, that the Croatian state assess whether one of the solutions would be moving the Serb and Croatian populations. When asked by the journalists whether the tanks had been summoned from Belgrade, Goran Hadzic replied: The tanks belong to the JNA and I can tell you that within the borders of the present Republic of Croatia the JNA is, if not in greater peril, then equally imperilled as the Serb people living there. They go there to liberate their colleagues, soldiers. "Reporter: When asked several times about who was invited to return to these regions, Hadzic expressed the wish for return not only of Serbs but of native Croats as well. Serb people did not endure genocide by the native Croats but by the colonists Ante Pavlovic brought to western Herzegovina, Croatian Zagorija and Imotsko. They were the first ones to raise arms and mine Serb houses. "In order to establish a normal life, we will have to present them with a return ticket. Hadzic also said Serbia should take care of women and children refugees and not of able-bodied men. Stating the data on SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, Goran Hadzic stressed there were 150.000 inhabitants living there and that its capital is Vukovar, which had not been liberated yet, but this does not mean it would not be. Goran Hadzic replied to the TASS reporter that his government offered 20 imprisoned guards to Croatian authorities in exchange for two missing Soviet journalists. Unfortunately, Hadzic said, 'our government does not know where they are.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So my question, Mr. Hadzic, did you hear your own words in this video or your words of the reporter as regards this offer for releasing two Soviet journalists?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard my words and I said "our government," meaning our federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that in the original, your words, or did you hear what the reporter stated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I heard in the original, "our government," at least that's the way it seemed to me. Perhaps we can play it again, just this last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we play perhaps just the last minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, my impression is that this was a woman's voice, so that's why I'm asking you whether you heard your own voice uttering this sentence that we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I was not focused. I heard it. It was the comment on the journalist, and it misconveyed the thing that I said earlier on. For Croatia, it was supposed to be "from Imotsko, from Hrvatska Zagorija [phoen]," and the preposition used was different. And it was "from western Herzegovina," not "into western Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Do you know that exchanges of prisoners were carried out during September and October? I mean in general. That they were carried out from when this decision of the Presidency was made and onwards.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they were carried out. And sporadically I was informed about this by Ilija Koncarevic, in terms of informal reports because he was not a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that we have here, that you are aware of, on the 25th of September the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was elected. Since you were the prime minister designate for that government, could you tell us how it was that you selected the people who you would propose as candidates for membership in that future government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were major problems involved for me personally. I had to meet certain requirements that were almost incompatible. First of all, territorial representation. But then also there should be professionalism, too. And often that was impossible to meet both requirements. So, as for all three parts of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, we wanted to have these three biggest parts represented, and then within these separate parts there should be representation of practically every village or every group of villages because it's different. If we, the so-called ministers, were to be elected in a different way, this would have caused great dissatisfaction among the population. So we needed people who were professionals but we also needed people who came from certain parts of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The candidates that you put forth, were all of these candidates members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not because membership in the SDS was not the main precondition or requirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As prime minister of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, did you have the authority to issue orders to some members of the government or, rather, to the ministers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any possibilities because I and the ministers were elected by the assembly, and we were held accountable by the assembly and we made decisions by voting at government sessions, and then these decisions had to be carried through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps remove a particular minister from his position?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not. If that minister would not agree with that, then it would have to be done by the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see L15, please. It is tab 1190. I think it is -- this translation does not correspond to the decision on election of the president, vice-presidents, and members of the government. Anyway, we can remove it from the screen. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask you about ministers who were in that government. I'm going to ask you to tell us a few words about them. One of the deputy prime ministers was Dr. Mladen Hadzic. Could you please tell us whether you knew him; and, if so, from when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. Mladen Hadzic originally hails from my village, but after he got his degree in medicine he no longer lived in Pacetin. He lived in Borovo Naselje. And then in the 1980s, he built a house in Tenja near Osijek. He moved to Tenja and lived there. He was president of the Serb Democratic Party in Tenja, of the local committee in Tenja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to inform my learned friend that if he would like to go to the decisions on election of the president and the government, those are in L1 at page 16 of the English. That's the complete Gazette for the period and it has all those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you to the Prosecution. If we may see L1, page 16 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I may have misspoke. That's the election of the president of the Great National Assembly I see, but the decision appointing the president of the government is at page 25. So that may be more in the area of the document. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, can you tell us since Dr. Mladen Hadzic had the same last name, like you, were you related?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had not been related over the past 200 years. Perhaps 300 years ago we were blood relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The second person on this list is Dragan Sabljakovic. Can you tell us something about him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was elected vice-president or vice premier on behalf of the local commune of Markusica. That is the biggest village in that part between Vinkovci and Osijek, and he did not really have any kind of professional education that would make him eligible for minister, so he was deputy prime minister in order to be able to deal with certain organisational matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ilija Kojic is the first one on this list of ministers. We've heard quite a bit about him already. Can you tell us whether he was a member of the Serb Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any information about him being a member of the SDS, so that means he wasn't. In Vukovar he wasn't. He certainly wasn't a member of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The second is Borislav Bogunovic. I believe that we've heard a lot about him so I won't be asking about him. The third is Bogdan Vojnovic. Can you tell us something about him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Bogdan Vojnovic; I knew him by name. He was the head of finance at Vupik. He was the best finance guy in the municipality of Vukovar. That was his reputation. That's why I tried to find him, and I did, and I asked him whether he would serve as minister, and he accepted the suggestion. He was not a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The next one is Vitomir Devetak. Again, can you tell us something about him? Just briefly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Vukasin Soskocanin was killed, he was the president of the local commune of Borovo Selo. Since Borovo Selo was the village with the highest number of population of all the villages in the area, they - and I mean the local commune - put forth the names of the people who were ministers or who would be ministers. Devetak was one of the three of them. He was put forth by people in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The next one is Slavko Dokmanovic. Can you tell us something about him, briefly? Missed a request colloquy?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the former president of Vukovar municipality. He was an agronomist from Trpinja, and he was not a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Vojin Susa.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a refugee from Vinkovci. Before the war, he was the assistant public prosecutor in Vinkovci. Together with a group of lawyers, he arrived in Dalj. Most of them were from Vukovar; i.e., from the municipality of Vukovar. They had agreed amongst themselves who could be the minister of justice, who could be the public prosecutor, and who could be president of the courts. I was not an expert, and I still don't know anything about the law and judiciary, so I really did not question their proposals. I accepted that Susa should become minister of justice, that Milos Vojnovic would be elected the president of a court. But that was later. Their plan was already on the table. They had drafted it amongst themselves. I'm not sure that Susa was a member of the SDS in Vinkovci. He may well have been, but I don't know. I never spoke to him as a party member. We were friends from school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mladen Jovic. Dr. Mladen Jovic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a physician from Borovo Selo. He came with the package, as it were. He was one on the list of the villagers of Borovo Selo. In Borovo Selo, there were a lot of Serbs who were not natives. They had moved from Bosna. They had to be represented, and their representative was Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that you've spoken about Ilija Petrovic at great length already. Can you tell us something about Milan Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Knezevic was a teacher from Baranja. He was a member of the Socialist Party of Croatia. He wore a double hat. He represented Baranja as well as the Socialist Party of Croatia. So those two requirements were met in one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Borivoje Milenkovic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Dalj. He was elected as a minister at the proposal of people from Dalj to represent them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Pajo Nedic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Bobota. He was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party. The locals of Bobota agreed that he should be minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Bogdan Vorkapic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Vukovar. He was a refugee in Prigrevica. He had arrived from Prigrevica at Dalj and became a minister. So he was not there when we sent out call-up papers. We called him personally because we needed him because he -- his professional profile fit the requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdan Vorkapic was not a member of the SDS. He never joined the SDS. He was a member of the socialist party, just like Milan Knezevic. He supported Martic in the elections and not me; so, in other words, he was my political opponent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Caslav Ocic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Caslav Ocic had a PhD in economics. He hailed from Dalj but lived in Belgrade. He belonged to the group of Serbs who were supposed to open a door for us in Belgrade in a way. Since Dalj is second largest village only to Borovo Selo, it gave two ministers: Caslav Ocic and Boro Milenkovic. That was also a proposal by the locals of Dalj. Later on he became a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Miomir Crnogorac.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my friend from Pacetin. We went to school together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The last on the list is Stevo Bogic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Borovo Selo. He came as a part of the package, together with Jovic and Devetak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can you tell us about the influence of the government; i.e., could the government exert any influence on the developments in the territory of SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That influence was negligible, if there was any at all. We did not have any technical capabilities and that really paints a very good picture of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the financial situation. What were the governments financial resources? Did it have a budget?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, when we were established -- or, rather, in those first few days or the first few months of our work, our bottom line was zero.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you and the other ministers receive any salaries? How much were they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of 1991, I did not receive a single salary, and I believe that the same was true for all the other ministers. Nobody was paid for what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government control any armed forces that would have been in a position to possibly enforce law or implement measures passed by the government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of the SBWS did not have any armed forces under its control. It didn't have any men under arms that it might have controlled, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We've had an occasion to hear in this courtroom that there was a service known as the Serbian national security. That service was headed by Stevo Bogic, who was directly subordinated to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. Stevo Bogic was a minister without a portfolio, and he was equal to me and all the others. He was elected by the assembly. I was the first among the equals. He was not subordinated to me. I could not give him any orders. And as far as his duties are concerned, in addition to the political ones that he had, he assumed a responsibility to set up a security service around the government building. That meant around-the-clock security detail in three shifts. And if a minister had to travel or be transferred somewhere, they had to be escorted or even driven because the ministers didn't have cars. If only one car was available, then a driver had to drive it. So it was more to do with driving people around than to provide security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that he organised the security detail for the government. What do you know about the functioning of the government's security detail? What was it? How many people were involved? What did they do? How they did it? As far as you can remember.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I was not in Slavonia and Baranja very often. In October, I was there only on two or three occasions, for two or three days. According to what I learned subsequently, Bogic established the security detail and recruited people from Borovo Selo mostly. According to what I know, there could not have been more than seven, eight, or nine of them; three in each of the shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When they worked, when they were on a shift, where were they, the three men that you just mentioned? Where would they spend their working hours, as it were?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out at the entrance into the manor and at the entrance into the courtyard. I don't know how things were organised during the night because I didn't go there during the night. Some of them even drove Stevo Bogic around. I used to see one or two of them with him outside Erdut, even.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where they were billeted? Where did they sleep?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never entered those rooms. However, there were two rooms there where they could sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You knew the people who were there who were standing guard around the government building. Did any of you [as interpreted] provide your security in 1991, 1992, and 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have a security detail. I didn't know them well at the time. I just greeted them at the entrance. I would just say good morning to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that your answer was not precise. You said that you didn't have a security detail. I asked you whether any of those men who secured the government facilities was part of your security detail.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had my security guards and it was none of them. When I attended government sessions, in formal terms, they were standing in front of the government building where the session was being held, but that had nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in the month of August 1991, Radovan Stojicic, Badza, came to SBWC [as interpreted] to take over the Territorial Defence and the police together with his unit. Did you - and I mean the government - have any impact on their actions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we couldn't influence their actions at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to influence Territorial Defence units that existed there or maybe the police that he took over? I mean, both you personally and the government.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We neither wanted to nor were -- nor had we the technical capacity to do it. And we didn't influence them at all. I can explain why we were technically unable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly because the government in Erdut had only one telephone which was connected to the Serbian network. It had a Belgrade telephone number. So we were able to communicate only with businesses in Serbia and families in Serbia. We were not able to use that telephone to contact people in SBWS. In the beginning, in September, only I had a car, a very old car that a Novi Sad bank gave me for my personal use. None of the other ministers had cars. But even that car was inadequate because we needed an all-terrain vehicle to reach many villages. I had to go across fields. So we had no communication with villages, with headquarters, with staffs. We didn't even have a fax machine. And even a fax machine wouldn't help us much because there were no fax machines on the other end in villages because there was no power. So we had no contact with these institutions and we couldn't influence them even if we had wanted to. It was all under Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was that situation with Arkan and his Volunteers Guard? Were you able to exert any influence on them? Were you able to give them any orders or instructions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't give them any orders or instructions, nor have I ever done that. They were either with Badza or with the military. They had no connection to our government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you talked about the relationship -- or, rather, the communication between your government and villages, could you tell us what was it like in Pacetin in 1992? Did any Territorial Defence exist there? How did it operate? To whom was it subordinated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that I myself am from Pacetin, I know what the situation was like there. In the early days when the village guards were formed, it was done independently, autonomously, or rather I should say spontaneously. As president of the local commune, I participated in their organisation and the entire Executive Council over which I presided, we were five or six members. It wasn't even called the Territorial Defence. It was later called the Village Defence Staff. In the beginning, we would stand guard in the centre of the village, and as the situation became more and more serious, we also placed guards along streets. So the village was open. Anybody who wanted to could pass, but people were just standing there, watching out for larger numbers of vehicles or buses because we were afraid of an attack. Later what I was practically blocked in Vukovar and could not longer return to Pacetin, I didn't dare to travel to Pacetin because I could be trapped there. I couldn't drive back in any weather. I didn't have a car that could travel on mud tracks. So later on my deputy took over those duties. Very soon in August when the army got involved more openly in that conflict, some unit from Nis arrived at Pacetin, according to the information I have, led by some colonel who took over the entire defence effort and all the rest. This is my indirect knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say this colonel of that unit from Nis took over, do you mean a JNA unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. He was a colonel of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us more precisely, what do you mean by "took over"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that the village guards and all the rest of the village organisation didn't have any purpose anymore. It was all placed under the command of the JNA. Maybe it's better to say under single command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to the situation in other villages? Was it similar to Pacetin or was it different somewhere?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I learned later, it was identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it is the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If that's convenient for you, Mr. Zivanovic. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About these village guards, these units, these defence staffs, and staffs of Territorial Defence, did they submit any reports on their work to the government or you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not, either to the government or myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the relationship between the government and the civilian local authorities, such as Executive Councils, in the municipalities of SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This situation was slightly idiosyncratic because Baranja remained intact and they were autonomous. The Executive Council functioned in Baranja independently without any consultations with the government. With the appointment of the president of their Executive Council, we only formally confirmed it because he was elected by their local assembly before any decision was made by the government. It was only after the liberation of Vukovar, I don't know how many days after the liberation, we proposed the president of the Executive Council for the municipality of Vukovar, and we appointed presidents also for Mirkovci village and Dalj later. These four municipalities, save for Baranja, were also in the process of being established, just like the government was, and they were not able to start working immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please D41. It is tab 1236.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, can you tell us to what extent was it possible for you to move at that time throughout the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to all the technical problems I described before the break - namely, that we had no resources, no cars, no fuel - there was also the practical problem that because of the military rule throughout the territory of SBWS, we were not able to move freely around the district, and there were also combat zones where we couldn't go at all because the Croatian army was there. So it was practically impossible. We could not even reach Western Srem. And in Eastern Slavonia, we somehow managed to pass through towards Dalj and Borovo Selo; although, in the early days, we also faced huge problems there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What were the problems you encountered as you tried to move through the district?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA set up check-points all over the district and it was necessary to have a permit to pass through. At some stage it became ridiculous, because every check-point asked for a different permit. Some ministers had to turn back and find a new permit before they were allowed to continue on their way. Sometimes you needed three different permits to go from my village, Pacetin, to Erdut. But that was later resolved. Things improved with time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the screen we can now see one document from the JNA granting permits for movement in the combat zones. In this respect, did members of the government of SBWS have any preferential treatment as officials? Did JNA treat them better in this respect than regular citizens?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early stages of the functioning of our government, we were treated all the same as any other citizens. We didn't have any preferential treatment. It didn't improve much over time. The only thing is that we had better communication in one part of the district between Bogota, Dalj, and Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We see in this document that it is not allowed to move around at night across the bridge towards Bogota -- sorry, Bogojevo without a permit. Was this applied? Was this enforced?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was enforced. But I didn't get any papers from them. And this is the first time, in fact, after I came to The Hague that I saw these documents. At that time, I didn't receive any documents from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask for an explanation, did you ask for this treatment to change, to allow you to move around freely?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ministers approached me every day describing the problems they had. And then I would contact the military command in Belgrade, and I talked to Kadijevic, and I managed, after surmounting many obstacles, to see him. But he showed so little understanding for our problems that my visit was futile, and I thought that I would get more understanding from Blagoje Adzic. But with him, it was exactly the same story as with Kadijevic. To this day, I don't know why they treated us that way. And only after the testimony of Aco Vasiljevic did I begin to understand why.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was it that you understood from his testimony?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I realised that they also had a feeling that I refused to co-operate with them, that I did not accept their officers, which is not true, because their officers never offered me any co-operation. It was not possible to co-operate because after that story with Nenezic, I didn't have any contact with officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned General Kadijevic and General Adzic. As you know, they had been marked as participants in the joint criminal enterprise. This is what I'd like to ask you. Apart from these meetings with both that you mentioned, what kind of contacts did you have with them, generally speaking, if any?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were contacts at my own initiative and they were very brief. I don't know if I ever stayed more than 15 or 20 minutes with either one of them. Later on I just saw them when they attended meetings of the Presidency concerning the Vance Plan, and then I never saw them again. And I didn't talk to them then. That was a big meeting. There were perhaps 30 of us there, or perhaps there were even 50 participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned these contacts that went on for 15 or 20 minutes, does that relate to the contacts that you mentioned a moment ago concerning freedom of movement through the region?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are the contacts where they refused me. They barely listened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other communication apart from that with them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any other communication with them. I didn't have their telephone numbers. I had no communication with them whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have already spoken about that contact, that telephone conversation with Slobodan Milosevic when the cease-fire agreement was supposed to be signed in September 1991. Could you tell us now what kind of contacts did you have with him before that or after that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that before that I had one contact. Perhaps in the month of September in 1991 when Professor Raskovic called me from Knin to be on this delegation of the Serb Democratic Party. I was the only person then from Slavonia, Baranja, and from Knin. Almost the entire Executive Board had come. Perhaps there were even 40 of them. He stood at the door then, we walked in, we all shook hands. As a matter of fact, I didn't even introduce myself by my name and surname. Perhaps just my surname. I didn't even say anything. As for that entire delegation, I think it was only Babic who spoke. That was not a long meeting either. That was the only time I saw him; the first time and the only time. After that, he phoned me after -- actually, during Wijnaendts' visit, and my understanding was that he called me because Wijnaendts had called him, telling him that I did not want to sign that. The next time I received a call from his office was when I was told that I should come to Belgrade in order to agree on this trip to Paris to the Dutch embassy there. I'm not sure whether it was to Paris or The Hague, but it was at the initiative of Henry Wijnaendts. I did not see him then. Babic and I met on the ground floor of this Presidency building so that we would agree how we would travel. We talked to his chief of protocol, Milosevic's chief of protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in this first meeting with Slobodan Milosevic, where you say that there was a big delegation consisting of 40 persons. Can you tell us what it was that was discussed then during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this had to do with that TV video-clip about Spegelj and this panic among the Serb people. He tried to pacify us in a way, not to have any kind of exodus take place, that there should be no panic either, that the JNA could protect us. But I'm not sure that there were any particular results there because this wasn't even discussed afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that meeting, did he address you directly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't even know who I was at the time and I didn't really matter. I think he didn't know any one of us except for Babic. Babic was the president of the municipality of Knin, so perhaps he was well known. But the rest of us were all anonymous. I'm not sure Professor Raskovic was with us. I'm not sure. I think it was only Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The other time when you came to the building where his office was and when you talked to that chief of protocol, can you tell us what this conversation consisted of, what the topic of this conversation was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the topic was preparing our trip for this meeting with Henry Wijnaendts and agreeing on the air flights, et cetera, because the federal government made it possible for us to travel by plane. This was agreed upon with the representatives of the European community, Henry Wijnaendts and Geert Ahrens. Because we had to fly from Belgrade. We did not have an airport in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat this name, Henry ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Henry Wijnaendts, or Wijnaendts, and Geert Ahrens. Mr. Ahrens. Ahrens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After that during 1991 and 1992, did you see Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After returning from one of these meetings that we went to, I don't know if it was Paris or The Hague, we were asked to come to see Milosevic. Babic was with me, and Caslav Ocic, who was my minister of foreign affairs in our government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. I'm not sure about this, but I think he was Babic's foreign minister, too, that was there. Professor Lazo Matsura. I'm not 100 per cent sure about him, but I think he was there. I saw then that Caslav Ocic knew them. They knew each other from the days of communism, because Caslav was a member of the city organisation of the League of Communists, but they were on two opposing sides in that conflict. I saw that they were not on very good terms, that they did not agree very much. But this is just a digression. It really has nothing to do with what I've been testifying about. Then Milosevic, after certain polite introductory remarks, said that the war should be over and that the Serbs in Croatia should get a status that would protect their rights. As he said, a type of executive, legislative, and parliamentary government and that this should be done within Croatia and that that would be a good thing for all. And that we should give this some thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. You mentioned three branches of government. Could you please repeat the ones that he mentioned to you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The executive, the legislative, and the judiciary. And our human rights should be protected and physically we should be protected, too. Along with international guarantees. Henry Wijnaendts, already in the couloirs of the meeting in Paris at the Dutch embassy there had suggested that to me, asking me what I thought about that. I said that I could accept that, but that he should first agree on that with Mr. Babic, because it would be hard for one side to accept that and the other one not so that would be a problem. Because then they could declare me a traitor, and then I said in jest I would have nowhere to go to. So when I heard Milosevic, I realised that he and Wijnaendts had already agreed on that because they had almost the same views as those that were communicated to me by Wijnaendts, because Wijnaendts said that to me at a smaller table that was close to the dining table where we had all been eating. So it was only the two of us at this small table and nobody else heard this. At this meeting with Milosevic, after all of these things were said, Babic changed his mood visibly. He got angry, and we quickly ended the meeting and left. I'm not sure now whether we had a press conference scheduled that afternoon or whether Babic hurried to schedule one. At any rate, we went to a press conference and Babic said that individuals from Serbia were pressuring us to remain in Croatia. I'm paraphrasing now. He said something along those lines. And it was obvious to the journalists, too, that that had been Milosevic. And then Milosevic said that we should agree on that. And now he said this without seeking any kind of agreement with me and that was unpleasant for me. And he said, "Ask Mr. Hadzic if you think that is not correct." So I made no special comment. Because he said that without seeking any kind of agreement with me - I mean, Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After this, did you have any other meetings with Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1991, I did not. I never met with him on my own. It's not that he ever received me only. I think that Babic and I came together when people started talking about the Vance Plan. And then he sent us to the government of Serbia to talk to some general, a retired general, who was head of a UN mission in Egypt. He would explain to us what the blue helmets were, how they operated, what their function was, and so on, so that I could learn more about that. Slavko Jovic was the name of that general. Further on in 1991, I was called a few times, not too many times, by Mr. Milosevic's secretary, first for a meeting with Marrack Goulding, the envoy for the secretary-general of UN, and after that Mr. Cyrus Vance, who the special envoy of the secretary-general of the UN. This was -- this discussion of the Vance Plan, concerning the adoption of the Vance Plan. In President Milosevic's office, once we were with Goulding, and this other time at the villa of the government of Serbia. It was called Boticeva Vila [phoen], and that is its name today as well. It is in Dedinje. Botic. Botic. The Botic villa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the indictment, Milan Martic is also mentioned as one of the participants of the joint criminal enterprise. Can you tell us when it was that you met him and can you tell us about your relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Milan Martic once came to Borovo Selo briefly to visit as minister of the SAO Krajina. He knew some active policemen who were from Vukovar and he was there as their guest. I saw him by chance there, and I met him, was introduced, and chatted for about five minutes perhaps. The second time I saw him was at a meeting of the Presidency of the SFRY concerning the acceptance of the Vance Plan. I don't remember seeing him otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did your relations develop later?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later I saw him at the assembly in Borovo Selo when the single republic of the Serb Krajina was formed and when I became president, and he was a minister in Zecevic's government. So I had a correct relationship with him, or rather no particular relationship. He was a minister in the government, I was the president of the republic, so we really had no points in common.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And later?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later we co-operated within the Supreme Defence Council when I was in Knin, but I wasn't in Knin very often. However, soon we clashed and, in my view, neither Martic nor I are to be blamed for that clash.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the nature of that conflict? What was this clash about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It escalated at this assembly session at Beli Manastir. But it began while I was attending negotiations in New York after the Croatian operation Maslenica. There were technical people on my delegation alongside myself, such as interpreters and members of our bureau, from Krajina, and they were in communication with the employees of the bureau who remained in Belgrade. And they received by fax a copy of an article from "Vecernje Novosti," a Belgrade newspaper, and one of the biggest head lines was about a statement given by Martic where he said Hadzic is promoting his own interests in New York, neglecting the people, and it was basically an attack on me by Martic. I called him on an open unsecure line from the US, and I asked, "Mile, what's the problem?" And he says, "You said about me that I am dense, stupid." I never said such a thing. So I asked, "Who told you that?" He said, "Some people from Belgrade told me, and I'm sure they're not lying." And that was the first step of our conflict. And it escalated after the so-called Croatian operation at Velebit, when Milan Martic off his own bat de-mined part of a minefield. I don't mean he did it himself. His police did it without the knowledge of the army or Mile Novakovic. That night the Croatian police took advantage of that open space, raided our territory, and perpetrated a massacre. They killed or slaughtered 19 of our fighting men in Lika. I told him he didn't have any right to do that and he has no right, nor does anybody, to do anything of their own initiative in a combat zone. Of course, he didn't answer anything. He didn't deny it, but he attacked me personally. That conflict escalated even further with the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about your relationship with Milan Babic, who is also named as one of the participants in the joint criminal enterprise: How long did you know him and how did your relationship evolve?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Milan Babic in May 1990 when, together with Boro Savic and another two of my friends, went to see Professor Raskovic to agree about the establishing of the SDS Vukovar. The professor met us in the municipal building in the office of Milan Babic. But Babic was not on the cabinet at that time, not yet, because everybody knows he's a -- he was a late sleeper, so he came after he got up around noon. And by that time we had finished talking, Dr. Raskovic and me, so I just exchanged greetings with him. We parted ways politically very soon after that because I was in the same camp as Professor Raskovic and he was in a different faction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another person cited in the indictment is Jovica Stanisic. Can you tell us something about him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I had no information on him whatsoever. His name cropped up sometime in 1991, but I had not met with him ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also heard the testimony of Witness GH-002, who said that in 1991 both you and he attended certain meetings with Stanisic. Is that correct? I don't know if you know who GH-002 is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move into private session for the moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I think we missed a part of your last intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked for the private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat, because it was not --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had no meeting with Jovica Stanisic or a joint meeting with GH-002 and Jovica Stanisic, but I can tell you how that witness came up with that and why he said it, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you met Franko Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't meet him in 1990, for sure. I even think that I didn't know him at all in the period for which I was indicted, 1992, 1993. I met him quite by chance in Ilok. One of my relatives stopped by in the street to greet me and she is the one who introduced us. But I'm not 100 per cent sure. That was in 1994. And I met him once again in a restaurant in Zemun. I don't know which of these encounters took place first, but I never co-operated with him. I never had any official meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I'm just warned that one -- our exhibit was -- was erroneously marked as 1D3658 at the page 25, line 22, of the transcript. And it was admitted into evidence as D130. The exact number of this document is 1D3568.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's noted, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The next in the group is Vojislav Seselj. When did you meet Mr. Seselj? What kind of relationship did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th March, there was a rally in Serbia. Vojislav Seselj was already a deputy. He -- and he appeared as a guest in Slavonia. He toured Serbian villages. He was in Pacetin as well. That's when I saw him first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's when I saw him, and I got to know him in a way, although I'm not even sure that he remembers me from that event. But I remember him. He was already a famous person. Since I was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party and he was in the Serbian Radical Party, he always showed animosity towards me. Whenever he came to Slavonia and Baranja, he had people with him who sided with him and he was very arrogant towards the rest of us. Later on we even had an open conflict, but that's a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell us something about the conflict. What was the conflict with Seselj about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It started when I supported the peace plan. The so-called Vance-Owen Plan of the international community for Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was a rally at the Sava congress centre where he attacked me and insulted me from the stage. I don't know why to this very day. I never communicated with him after that, or at least not until the moment we were both detained here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already asked you about Stojicic and Kadijevic, as well as Adzic. There are two more names that we have not discussed at all. One of them is Radmilo Bogdanovic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radmilo Bogdanovic was the minister of the interior of Serbia, and later he was the president of a security council of some sort. I remember that, but I don't remember that I ever actually met him in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please repeat what Mr. Bogdanovic became once he was no longer the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt that from the media. He was the president of the assembly committee on security in the Serbian assembly where he was an MP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the last name is that of Mihalj Kertes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mihalj Kertes married a girl from my village. However, that woman, or, rather, her parents lived in Ilok. She was born in Ilok herself but her father hails from my village. Her father is my aunt's brother or my uncle's wife's brother. We are not blood relatives, in other words, but we knew each other. I was not on very good terms with Kertes, to put it mildly. We almost did not communicate after that meeting in Backa Palanka which took place in May when he cursed everybody who spoke to Koncarevic and Petrovic who were in communication with the two of them. I continued communicating with both Koncarevic and Petrovic. I didn't want to listen to Kertes, and he held it against me. Later on a majority of the attacks on me and slander came from that source. You will remember when I mentioned Trivo Ivkovic and others. If it were not tragic, it would be funny. Those anecdotes involved 50 pistols, millions of German marks, and so on and so forth, and they all come from the same source.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to mention the last name on the list. It's the same of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. You've already said quite a lot about him. I suppose you will continue talking about him later. And now I'm just going to read the names on the list of the Serbian forces. That's also in the indictment, Count 11. I will ask you to tell me whether you had contact with any part of those forces. Were any of those segments subordinated to you? The first part are members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in no position at all to order anything to the JNA or even talk to them or make some arrangements with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on the JNA became the Army of Yugoslavia and it was known under its name. And during the period covered by the indictment, were you in command of any of the segments of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Under B, we can see the newly established Serbian Territorial Defence in the SAO Krajina. Were you ever in a position to give them orders?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Because they were under the government of the SAO Krajina under Milan Babic, if I understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the Territorial Defence of the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In our region, the Territorial Defence was different than the Territorial Defence in the SAO Krajina. We did not have any sort of command over them. We did not control them, we could not give them orders, we were not in communication with them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The subsequently established Serbian army of Krajina is something you're familiar with; right? Did you exert command or control over that military?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never in a position to be in command of the Serbian army of Krajina. I was a member of a body whose name escapes me. It was the Council of the Supreme Command or something to the effect. The name escapes me, but it will come back to me in a minute or two. Together with me, members were the commander of the army, the minister of defence, and the minister of the police. I represented the government. The body was called the Supreme Military Council. I apologise. So I was in a minority with regard to the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One part of your answer has been misrecorded in the transcript. When you said something about the government, it says that you represented the government.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was an equal member of the Supreme Defence Council. The commander of the Serbian army of Krajina, Mile Novakovic, was also there, the prime minister, Djordje Begovic was a member. Minister Stojan Spanovic, and Minister Milan Martic. The government had an absolute majority there. If I remember the situation well, those were legal and professional issues that I didn't know much about. I didn't understand those issues too well, so I didn't want to meddle too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your role; i.e., did you have under your command a Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
